chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Safwan ibn Yahya from 'Isa ibn al-Qasim said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who went out in the month of Ramadan while his companions were eating suhoor (pre-dawn meal) in a house. He looked at the dawn and called them. Some of them stopped, and some thought he was mocking them, so they ate. He said: 'He completes his fast and also makes up for it (qada).'.

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And whoever thought that the sun had set due to a cloud or something similar, and broke his fast, then it became clear that it had not actually set at that time, it is obligatory upon him to make up the fast. What he mentioned (may Allah have mercy on him) is the narration of Samaan ibn Mihran in the narration of Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Samaan and Abu Basir, and no one else narrated it.

key_terms.شَاهِد: Witness/Observer (implied context of seeing the sun)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if someone breaks their fast thinking the sun has set, but it turns out it was still up?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between *qada* (making up the fast) and *kaffarah* (expiation) for those who break their fast due to honest error (*ghalat*) or doubt (*shakk*) regarding sunset. It highlights the Shia juristic principle that mere uncertainty or reasonable assumption, such as mistaking clouds for sunset or misinterpreting a companion's intent, does not incur the heavier penalty of *kaffarah*, provided the person did not act with deliberate disregard. The text further notes the specific chain of transmission (*isnad*) involving Samaan ibn Mihran, underscoring the reliability of this ruling within the school of al-Tusi.
